position.headline: ONSET measures facial movement. It cannot tell you whether someone is lying.
can: Detect and time brief facial movements and say which action-unit pattern they most resemble, with uncertainty.
Report how often such movements occurred in a stretch of video - rates corrected for the time each facial region was actually observable, with exact confidence intervals.
Compare two stretches of the same recording (for example a baseline question and a target question) with tests that suit small counts and that are corrected for the number of comparisons made.
Show what a hypothetical detector with a given effect size would achieve at a given base rate.
cannot: Establish that a person is lying or telling the truth.
Turn a movement count or an AU pattern into a probability of deception.
Say what the person felt or intended.
Support any decision about a person: employment, legal, immigration, security, education.
why: No facial cue with validated individual-level accuracy was found among the sources opened for this build. The best-known candidate, the micro-expression, is rare and also occurs in people telling the truth.
Base rates: when lies are uncommon, even a detector that is right 90% of the time on each class produces mostly false accusations (calculator below).

Confounds: talking, chewing, thinking, blinking, being filmed, culture and personality all move the face. A within-person baseline is the minimum for any comparison, and even then the difference has many causes.
Ground truth: a study needs to know who lied. Instructed, low-stakes lies are easy to collect and differ from high-stakes deception; verified high-stakes ground truth is scarce.
instead: A behavioural-cue instrument: measure observable movement per segment, test pre-registered hypotheses, report effect sizes with intervals, and say 'differs' - never 'lied'.
A teaching instrument: let the user see how base rates, small counts and many comparisons produce confident but empty conclusions.

evidence.onset_measure: Event count and rate per minute, duration, action-unit pattern (Bench, Evidence).
evidence.claim: Leaked micro-expressions reveal concealed emotion, and so reveal lying.
known: Rare in the one high-stakes data set coded in detail: 2% of about 700 expressions were micro-expressions (Porter & ten Brinke 2008, as reported by Burgoon 2018).
A later analysis counted six among people who were deceiving and eight among genuine pleaders, so they occurred in both groups (as reported by Burgoon 2018).
Untrained observers could not separate truth from deception with them (Porter et al. 2012, as reported by Burgoon 2018).
evidence.assessment: Occurrence is real but rare and not specific to lying. Finding one proves nothing; finding none proves nothing.
evidence.status_text: Not supported by the evidence found

ref_details.cite: Burgoon, J. K. (2018). Microexpressions are not the best way to catch a liar. Frontiers in Psychology, 9, 1672.
ref_details.finding: Opinion article arguing that micro-expression theory's propositions mostly fail; proposes the 'rigidity effect' (reduced movement under high stakes) as an alternative to be tested.

ref_details.cite: Porter, S., & ten Brinke, L. (2008). Reading between the lies: Identifying concealed and falsified emotions in universal facial expressions. Psychological Science.
ref_details.finding: Figures used here (2% of about 700 high-stakes expressions were micro-expressions) are as reported by Burgoon (2018); the original article was not opened.

evidence.cue: Human lie detection from behaviour in general
evidence.onset_measure: Not measured; context for every other row.
evidence.claim: Trained or attentive people can tell lies from truth by watching behaviour.
known: Across 206 documents and 24,483 judges, 54% of lie/truth judgments were correct: 47% of lies and 61% of truths were identified (Bond & DePaulo 2006).
evidence.assessment: A statement about human judges, not a proof that no algorithm could do better - but nothing opened for this build shows that one can, with real stakes and unseen people.
evidence.status_text: Validated limit - a well-supported finding about what cannot be concluded

ref_details.cite: Bond, C. F., Jr., & DePaulo, B. M. (2006). Accuracy of deception judgments. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 10(3), 214-234.
ref_details.finding: Meta-analysis of 206 documents and 24,483 judges: 54% of lie/truth judgments were correct (47% of lies and 61% of truths identified).

evidence.cue: Reduced overall movement ('rigidity') under high stakes
evidence.onset_measure: Movement activity per facial region and segment, excluding blinks and speech (Cue Lab, segment study).
evidence.claim: Liars move the face less, as they over-control their behaviour.
known: Proposed by Burgoon (2018) as an alternative to micro-expressions. In one experiment guilty participants showed rigidity on 8 of 10 facial movements measured (Pentland et al. 2017, as reported by Burgoon 2018).
The same article says the causal mechanism is unresolved and needs experiments.
evidence.assessment: Interesting and testable, at an early stage. Reduced movement also follows from nervousness, concentration, instructions to stay still, or simply from the person's habits.
evidence.status_text: Research hypothesis - proposed, not validated for individuals

ref_details.cite: Burgoon, J. K. (2018). Microexpressions are not the best way to catch a liar. Frontiers in Psychology, 9, 1672.
ref_details.finding: Opinion article arguing that micro-expression theory's propositions mostly fail; proposes the 'rigidity effect' (reduced movement under high stakes) as an alternative to be tested.

evidence.cue: Smiles and other positive expressions while answering
evidence.onset_measure: AU6 / AU12 events and their rate (Bench).
evidence.claim: A smile at the wrong moment signals deceit (or its absence signals truth).
known: Burgoon (2018) notes that felt emotion and expression do not map one-to-one and that smiles and other expressions occur in both liars and truth-tellers.
evidence.assessment: Smiles are frequent, social and context-driven; they are not a diagnostic of anything but a smile.
evidence.status_text: Not supported by the evidence found

ref_details.cite: Burgoon, J. K. (2018). Microexpressions are not the best way to catch a liar. Frontiers in Psychology, 9, 1672.
ref_details.finding: Opinion article arguing that micro-expression theory's propositions mostly fail; proposes the 'rigidity effect' (reduced movement under high stakes) as an alternative to be tested.

evidence.cue: A facial configuration shows the emotion behind it
evidence.onset_measure: Category hypotheses derived from AU evidence (Bench). They are labelled as hypotheses.
evidence.claim: Reading the AU pattern reveals what the person feels.
known: Burgoon (2018) summarises a study in which most participants who reported a given emotion did not show the matching action units, and none of the participants who reported surprise showed the prototypical display.
Barrett et al. (2019) review this at length (not opened in this build).
evidence.assessment: ONSET's category labels are conveniences for comparing with annotated data sets, not statements about feelings.

ref_details.finding: Opinion article arguing that micro-expression theory's propositions mostly fail; proposes the 'rigidity effect' (reduced movement under high stakes) as an alternative to be tested.

ref_details.cite: Barrett, L. F., Adolphs, R., Marsella, S., Martinez, A. M., & Pollak, S. D. (2019). Emotional expressions reconsidered: Challenges to inferring emotion from human facial movements. Psychological Science in the Public Interest.
ref_details.finding: Not opened in this build (its record was refused by the fetch proxy). Review of what facial movements do and do not reveal about emotion.

evidence.onset_measure: Blink events and rate per minute, exposure-corrected (Cue Lab).
evidence.claim: Lying changes how often a person blinks.
known: No source on blinking and deception was opened for this build.
evidence.assessment: Left as an open hypothesis to be read up and, if pursued, pre-registered. ONSET measures blinks mainly because they are the largest confound for the eye region.
evidence.status_text: Research hypothesis - proposed, not validated for individuals

evidence.onset_measure: Not measured (only a conjugate-gaze shift of the lids is modelled as a nuisance).
known: Widely held as a folk belief and reviewed in the deception literature (see Vrij et al. 2019 and DePaulo et al. 2003 - neither was opened in this build, so no figure is quoted here).
evidence.assessment: Not offered. Treat any tool that scores gaze aversion as evidence of lying with suspicion until you have read the reviews.
evidence.status_text: Not supported by the evidence found

ref_details.cite: DePaulo, B. M., Lindsay, J. J., Malone, B. E., Muhlenbruck, L., Charlton, K., & Cooper, H. (2003). Cues to deception. Psychological Bulletin.
ref_details.finding: Not opened in this build. A meta-analysis of cues to deception; read it for effect sizes per cue.

ref_details.cite: Vrij, A., Hartwig, M., & Granhag, P. A. (2019). Reading lies: Nonverbal communication and deception. Annual Review of Psychology.
ref_details.finding: Not opened in this build. Review of nonverbal cues to deception.

evidence.cue: Speech, chewing, laughter, nodding, posture shifts
evidence.onset_measure: Flagged and excluded: mouth-movement windows, head excursion, sustained displacement.
evidence.claim: (None - these are the reasons naive movement counts differ between two stretches of video.)
known: On the synthetic phantoms used to calibrate ONSET, ordinary blinks, speech and head motion produce far larger movement signals than any scripted micro-movement. The instrument labels them rather than hiding them.
evidence.assessment: Any comparison between segments must be balanced for them or restricted to times when they are absent.
evidence.status_text: Confound - real movement with non-deceptive causes

evidence.claim: Training people (or models) to recognise micro-expressions improves lie detection.
known: Recognising posed expressions in images is a different skill from telling lies from truths in real behaviour; no source showing a lie-detection benefit was opened for this build.
evidence.assessment: Do not infer lie-detection value from improved expression-recognition scores, human or machine.
evidence.status_text: Not supported by the evidence found

bottom_line: Among the sources opened during this build, none established a facial cue that identifies deception for an individual. Population-level differences, where reported, are small, context-dependent, or still hypotheses. The responsible output of this module is therefore a measurement and a test, never a verdict.

status_text.unsupported: Not supported by the evidence found

regulation.text: A face video is personal data. Collect it only with informed, revocable consent for a stated purpose, keep it only as long as needed, and get your institution's ethics approval before recording other people. (Check your national law, for example India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and your institution's rules.)

protocol.text: State one hypothesis per cue before recording (for example: 'blink rate differs between the baseline and the target segment'), and the smallest difference you would care about.
Design a procedure that creates known ground truth (for example a staged-scenario paradigm with verified statements), and say how closely its stakes resemble the situation you care about.
Record a within-person baseline in the same room, lighting and posture, with the same task demands.
Counterbalance the order of segments and questions across participants; randomise who is asked what, so segment effects are not time or fatigue effects.
Plan the number of participants and events beforehand. A handful of events per segment cannot reach significance (the audit shows the exact minimum).
Annotate or detect speech, blinks and head motion, and analyse them as covariates or exclude them symmetrically in both segments.
Pre-register the cues, the test, the exclusion rules and the correction for multiple comparisons. Everything else is exploratory and must be labelled so.
Evaluate any predictive model on participants it has never seen (subject-independent), never on other clips of the same person.
Report positive and negative predictive values at the base rates of the intended use, not only accuracy on a balanced sample.
Report effect sizes with confidence intervals, including for results that did not reach significance.
Obtain ethics approval and informed consent, including consent to the specific analysis; give participants the right to withdraw their video.
Decide in advance what the result may and may not be used for. Individual decisions about people are outside what this evidence can support.
